blocks.value: **The wildcard argument represents an unknown type and is specified by the question mark.** Wildcards allow greater control of the types you use, and fall into two categories: **unbounded** and **bounded**.
**`<?>` denotes an unbounded wildcard, used to represent any type.**
The method prints a list of any type. Note the loop variable is `Object`, with an unbounded wildcard, that is all the compiler knows the elements to be.

`List<?>` is not the same as `List<Object>`. A `List<String>` **can** be passed to `List<?>`, but **cannot** be passed to `List<Object>`: one of the more surprising rules in Java, and the reason wildcards exist at all.

To relax restrictions on a variable, use an **upper bounded wildcard**, which **restricts the unknown type to a specific type or a subtype of that type**. Declare it with `?` followed by **`extends`** and its upper bound:
Because every element is guaranteed to be a `Number` or a subtype, the loop variable can be `Number` and `doubleValue()` can be called, neither of which would work with `<?>`.
A **lower bounded wildcard restricts the unknown type to a specific type or a super type of that type**, expressed with `?` followed by **`super`** and its lower bound.

Suppose you want a method that puts `Integer` objects into a list. To maximise flexibility, it should work on anything that can hold `Integer` values, `Integer`, `Number`, or `Object`. Specify `List<? super Integer>`:

items: If the parameter **produces** values you read out of it, use **`extends`**.
If the parameter **consumes** values you put into it, use **`super`**.

blocks.value: `sumOfList` reads numbers out, so it is a producer: `extends`. `addNumbers` writes integers in, so it is a consumer: `super`. That single mnemonic settles nearly every case.
